memoryText: Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Philippians 4:6-7 slowly, several times, and try to say it from memory. Then read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
These verses are Paul’s prescription for anxiety. They are written by a man in prison.

“Do not be anxious about anything.” The command is wide: about anything. Paul does not say that we will never feel worry, but that we should not live in it. Anxiety divides the mind and assumes that everything depends on us.

“But in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving.” The alternative to worry is prayer. Prayer is the general word; supplication is the specific asking for needs. Thanksgiving is included, because it reminds us of God’s faithfulness in the past and shifts our focus from what we lack.

“Let your requests be made known to God.” Be specific. God knows already, but he invites us to say it. Bring the actual worries by name.

“And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.” Notice the promise: it is not that the circumstances will necessarily change but that peace will stand guard like a soldier at the gate. It is a peace that does not make sense from the outside. It is found “in Christ Jesus.”

When anxiety rises, pray this verse, and turn each worry into a request with thanks.
weekInReview: This week you moved from Ephesians into Philippians and Colossians. Psalms 68 and 110 showed the ascended Christ, who leads captives, gives gifts, and sits at God’s right hand as priest-king. Philippians showed joy in prison: the gospel advances through chains, Christ is the model of humility, and God works in us both to will and to work. A doctrinal pause on the Christ hymn considered that Jesus is fully God and fully man in one person, who emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and was exalted to the name above every name. Philippians 3 and 4 showed the surpassing worth of knowing Christ, pressing on toward the goal, praying instead of worrying, and the secret of contentment in Christ who strengthens us. Colossians 1 and 2 presented the supremacy of Christ: image of the invisible God, creator and sustainer of all things, head of the church, reconciler by the blood of his cross, and Christ in us, the hope of glory.
reflectionQuestions: Paul says to be anxious about nothing and to pray about everything. What is one worry you need to turn into a specific prayer right now? Take a few minutes and do it.
Colossians 1:15-20 says Christ is supreme over creation and over the church. Where in your life do you treat Christ as less than preeminent? What would it look like to give him first place?

Philippians 3 says Paul counted all his credentials as loss for the sake of knowing Christ. What do you trust in besides Christ for your standing, identity, or security? What would it look like to let it go?
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for being supreme and for being your peace.
Thank him for the peace of God that guards your heart and mind.
